title: The Big-Bang singularity
one_line_summary: Sketches, in Geroch's style, a cosmological singularity theorem: a Cauchy slice guarantees maximal timelike curves, maximal curves must be normal geodesics free of focal points, gravity plus an energy condition forces the normal congruence to focus within proper time 3/c0, so no event can lie farther than 3/c0 from the slice; run backwards in an expanding Friedmann universe this makes every past-directed timelike curve run out of spacetime, which is the Big Bang.
role_in_book: The final chapter of the book and a deliberate bookend: Part III (Chapters 15-19) found a = 0 in explicit Friedmann solutions but left open whether that was an artefact of perfect homogeneity. Here the tools of Part V (covariant derivative commutators and the Ricci tensor from Chapter 35, projection tensors from Chapter 39) and the energy conditions of Chapter 13 are combined into a global, symmetry-light argument that a past singularity is generic. It closes the book by returning to the beginning of the Universe, previews the global (causal-structure) methods of Penrose, Hawking and Geroch that the book otherwise omits, and uses the exercises to introduce the Raychaudhuri equation, the standard engine of singularity theorems.

assumed_background.topic: Geodesics as curves of extremal interval; timelike geodesics maximize proper time; conjugate points spoil extremality
Covariant derivative, semicolon notation, torsion-free symmetric connection coefficients
Commutator of covariant derivatives gives the Riemann tensor (eqn 35.13); contraction to Ricci
Ricci tensor as the part of curvature that shrinks volumes of freely falling balls
Einstein field equation in trace-reversed form, geometric units G = c = 1
Energy conditions on the energy-momentum tensor
Robertson-Walker metric, scale factor a(t), cosmic time, Friedmann models and their initial a = 0
Perpendicular distance from a point to a line or surface is the shortest
Separable first-order ODEs and finite-time blow-up of dy/dx = y^2
Trace of a symmetric matrix, eigenvalues, sum of squares versus square of sum
Expansion of the Universe and the Hubble parameter

learning_objectives: Reader can state the question the chapter answers: whether the initial singularity of Friedmann models survives without exact homogeneity and isotropy.

Reader can explain, with a Euclidean sketch, why the shortest path from a point to a surface must hit the surface at a right angle and why a normal geodesic that has crossed a neighbour is no longer shortest.
Reader can translate those Euclidean facts into Lorentzian ones, replacing shortest by longest proper time, and say why the sign of the metric causes the swap.

Reader can build the unit normal geodesic congruence of a spacelike hypersurface from a proper-time function phi and prove from u_mu = grad phi that the congruence is geodesic and has symmetric u_{mu;nu}.
Reader can define the convergence c = -u^mu_{;mu} and interpret its sign as volume shrinking or growing along the flow.
Reader can reproduce the derivation of dc/dtau = u^{nu;alpha}u_{alpha;nu} + R_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu using the Ricci identity and the geodesic property.
Reader can split u_{alpha;nu} into trace and trace-free parts with the projection tensor and prove u^{nu;alpha}u_{alpha;nu} >= c^2/3.

Reader can identify the energy condition actually needed for R_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu >= 0 (the strong energy condition, rho + 3p >= 0 for a perfect fluid) and note that the text labels it the weak condition.
Reader can integrate dc/dtau >= c^2/3 to show convergence must diverge by tau = 3/c0 and explain why this means a caustic forms.
Reader can assemble the proof by contradiction: maximal curves exist (Cauchy surface) yet cannot exist beyond 3/c0 (focusing), so spacetime cannot extend that far.
Reader can compute c = -3 a-dot/a for comoving dust, explain why the argument fails to the future but applies to the past, and evaluate the past bound 3/c0 = 1/H0.
Reader can explain what 'singularity' means in this argument (timelike curves that cannot be continued within a smooth manifold) and how that differs from a statement about infinite density.
Reader can derive the Raychaudhuri equation with expansion, shear and rotation (exercises) and show focusing follows when rotation vanishes and the strong energy condition holds.

teaching_approach.summary: A compressed proof sketch of a singularity theorem, told in the book's chatty register. The authors avoid the full causal-structure apparatus by stating two 'geometric facts' in ordinary Euclidean 3-space, flipping them to Lorentzian form with a single word change (longest for shortest), and then doing the one genuinely local calculation (how the convergence of the normal congruence evolves) inside two boxed Examples. An inequality from a trace/trace-free split plus an energy condition gives a Riccati-type differential inequality whose finite-time blow-up delivers a contradiction. The payoff is staged as disappointment and rescue: the result seems useless for an expanding universe until time is run backwards. The book ends on a literary flourish, with the Universe (and the text) starting with a bang, while the standard Raychaudhuri machinery is left to the exercises.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: is the Big Bang of Robertson-Walker/Friedmann models a symmetry artefact or a robust prediction?

Assumption laid down: take a constant-cosmic-time slice that is a Cauchy surface; compactness of causal curves then guarantees a longest timelike curve from the slice to any event in its domain of dependence.

Warm-up in Euclidean space: the shortest route from a point to a surface meets it orthogonally; a normal geodesic that has crossed another cannot be shortest because the corner can be cut (the crossing is a conjugate point, recalling Chapter 8).
Transfer to spacetime: straightest timelike lines are longest, so the same facts hold with longest in place of shortest.
Model: a proper-time-from-S function phi, its gradient u, proof that u is a unit geodesic field, and definition of the convergence c.
Formalism, Example 50.1: differentiate c along u, trade derivative order via the Ricci identity, integrate by parts, and drop the geodesic term to get a square term plus a Ricci term.
Formalism, Example 50.2: project out the trace with P and show the square term is at least c^2/3.
Physics input: the trace-reversed Einstein equation plus an energy condition make the Ricci term non-negative, giving dc/dtau >= c^2/3 (gravity focuses).
Check/consequence: integrate to show c diverges by tau = 3/c0; interpret as a caustic where normal geodesics cross.
Logical clincher: existence of longest curves versus their impossibility past 3/c0 forces the conclusion that no event lies farther than 3/c0 from S.
Application: for Friedmann dust c = -3 a-dot/a is negative, so the theorem fails to the future; reversing time makes it apply to the past.
Interpretation: past-directed timelike curves must end within 3/c0 because they hit a point excised from the smooth manifold; this is the Big-Bang singularity, and the book closes.
Exercises extend to the full Raychaudhuri equation with shear and rotation and the strong energy condition.
signature_moves: Proxy geometry: argue the key extremal facts with pictures in flat Euclidean space, then reverse the inequality for Lorentzian signature instead of proving them in spacetime.

Gradient trick: define the congruence as the gradient of a proper-time function so that symmetry of u_{mu;nu}, the geodesic property and zero rotation all come for free, which lets the text skip shear-free/rotation bookkeeping that the exercises then restore.
Heavy algebra quarantined in boxed Examples followed by a 'pause and interpret' paragraph that reads each term physically (volume shrinking by Ricci, a positive square).
Identities needed for the decomposition are listed in a footnote as numbered 'facts' and pushed into Exercise 50.1, turning text gaps into guided homework.
Contradiction as the engine: two statements that cannot both hold (maximal curves exist; maximal curves cannot exist beyond 3/c0) are reconciled only by cutting spacetime short.
Disappointment-then-rescue staging in §50.3: the result looks inapplicable to an expanding universe until time is reversed.
Literary bookends: a Lucretius epigraph about the heavens having a birth and a closing line that inverts a famous poetic ending, marking the end of the book.

sections.title: Chapter opening: is the Big Bang an artefact?
sections.summary: Frames the chapter's question (is the Friedmann initial singularity physical or an idealization) and announces the answer: under mild assumptions a past singularity is realistic and perhaps unavoidable. Introduces a constant-cosmic-time slice assumed to be a Cauchy surface, together with its domain of dependence, and asserts that a longest timelike curve then exists from the slice to any event in that domain. Margin notes credit Geroch's lecture notes for the form of the argument, point to Penrose, Wald and Hawking-Ellis, and justify the existence claim by compactness of the space of causal curves.
concepts: existence of a maximal timelike curve
compactness of the space of causal curves
key_moves: Pose the artefact-versus-reality question about the Friedmann singularity.
Assume the present slice is a Cauchy surface.
Invoke compactness to guarantee a proper-time-maximizing curve from the slice to any event in its domain of dependence.

sections.title: Facts about Euclidean geometry
sections.summary: Uses ordinary 3-space as a rehearsal. Among all geodesics from a point to a surface S, the shortest must meet S at a right angle, since a slanted one can be beaten by a perpendicular one (Fig. 50.1); these are called orthogonal or normal geodesics. Next, if two normal geodesics cross at a point r, then the one continuing past r to a point q cannot be the shortest route from q to S: follow it to near r, cut across to the other geodesic and ride that down (Fig. 50.2). The crossing is identified with the conjugate points of Chapter 8, beyond which a trajectory stops being a minimum.
concepts: orthogonality of the shortest path to a surface
key_moves: Shortest path to a surface is a normal geodesic (first-variation fact).
A normal geodesic continued past a crossing with another normal geodesic is not minimizing, by rounding the corner.
Tie the crossing point to the conjugate-point criterion of Chapter 8.

sections.title: Orthogonal geodesics in spacetime
sections.summary: Moves to spacetime, where timelike geodesics maximize proper time, so the Euclidean facts carry over with longest replacing shortest. A proper-time-from-S function phi is introduced, and its gradient defines a unit timelike field u whose covariant derivative is symmetric; this makes u automatically geodesic, the tangent to all normal geodesics. The convergence c = -div u is defined. Example 50.1 differentiates c along u, uses the Ricci identity and the geodesic property to get a square of u_{alpha;nu} plus a Ricci term; Example 50.2 uses the projection tensor to show the square is at least c^2/3. The trace-reversed Einstein equation and an energy condition make the Ricci term non-negative, giving dc/dtau >= c^2/3, whose integral blows up by tau = 3/c0: a caustic forms and normal geodesics must cross. Combined with the two geometric facts, this contradicts the existence of maximal curves unless no event lies farther than 3/c0 from S along a timelike curve.
concepts: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
symmetry of the second covariant derivative of a scalar
trace and trace-free decomposition of the velocity gradient
trace inequality for the velocity gradient
existence of a maximal timelike curve
key_moves: Swap shortest for longest because of the Lorentzian sign of the metric.
Set u_mu = grad_mu phi with u.u = -1; symmetry of u_{nu;mu} gives u^mu u_{nu;mu} = (1/2)(u.u)_{;nu} = 0, so u is geodesic.
Define c = -u^mu_{;mu}.
Example 50.1: Ricci identity contracted on alpha and mu converts u^alpha_{;alpha nu} into u^alpha_{;nu alpha} minus a Ricci term; integrate by parts; the geodesic term vanishes.
Example 50.2: write u_{alpha;nu} = -(c/3)P + trace-free part; cross terms vanish because the trace-free part is orthogonal to P; drop the non-negative trace-free square.
Use R_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu = 8 pi (T - (1/2) g T)u u >= 0 to reach dc/dtau >= c^2/3.
Integrate: c(tau) >= 3/(3/c0 - tau), diverging by tau = 3/c0.
Divergent convergence means neighbouring normal geodesics cross (caustic), so they stop being maximal.
Contradiction with the Cauchy-surface existence result: events more than 3/c0 from S cannot exist.

sections.title: Our Universe
sections.summary: Applies the result to a near-Friedmann perfect-fluid universe. A comoving volume grows as a^3, so the convergence of the comoving dust world lines is c = -3 a-dot/a, negative for an expanding universe; the theorem therefore says nothing about the future. Reversing the time direction flips the sign, so with S the present slice no past-directed timelike curve can be longer than 3/c0. Because the theory lives on a smooth manifold, the place such curves would reach is not part of the manifold: it is a point that has to be excised (Fig. 50.4). That missing boundary is the initial Big-Bang singularity, which the authors present as inevitable for universes like ours, closing the book.
concepts: convergence of comoving Friedmann world lines
time reversal of the focusing argument
key_moves: Read convergence as minus the fractional rate of change of comoving volume, V proportional to a^3, giving c = -3 a-dot/a.
Observe the future-directed argument fails because c < 0 in an expanding universe.
Reverse time: past-directed convergence is +3 a-dot/a > 0, so the bound applies to the past.
Interpret the bound as timelike curves leaving the smooth manifold: the singular point is removed from spacetime.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: Four summary bullets restate the chain Cauchy surface, 3/c0 bound, singularity, Big Bang. Three exercises follow: properties of the projection tensor (including the spacelike-normal version), a guided derivation of the Raychaudhuri equation for a timelike geodesic congruence with its decomposition into expansion, shear and rotation (following Zee), and a proof that with zero rotation and the strong energy condition the congruence is focused.
key_moves: Recast the chapter's calculation in the conventional Raychaudhuri language with theta = -c.
Show the shear square is non-negative when the tensor is purely spatial and rotation vanishes.
Combine with the strong energy condition to get d theta/d tau <= -theta^2/3.

concepts.name: Big-Bang singularity
concepts.definition: The past boundary of an expanding universe at which every past-directed timelike world line comes to an end after finite proper time, because the events it would reach cannot belong to a smooth spacetime manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed at the outset as either an artefact of Friedmann symmetry or a real event, and established at the end by running the focusing argument backwards in time from today's slice; pictured as a hole cut out of a drawn sheet (Fig. 50.4).
concepts.notes: The argument establishes incompleteness of past timelike curves; that curvature or density diverges there is known from the explicit Friedmann solutions, not from this theorem.

concepts.name: cosmological singularity theorem
aliases: focusing theorem for a Cauchy slice
concepts.definition: If spacetime is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface S, the strong energy condition holds, and the convergence of the future-directed unit normals to S is everywhere at least c0 > 0, then no future-directed timelike curve from S has proper length exceeding 3/c0; the time-reversed version applies to expanding universes and bounds the past.
concepts.how_introduced: Never named as a theorem; built as a chain of plausibility arguments: existence of maximal curves, Euclidean normal-geodesic facts transplanted to spacetime, the convergence evolution equation, integration of the inequality, and contradiction.
prerequisites: existence of a maximal timelike curve
concepts.notes: The book follows Geroch's lecture-note version; the full statement needs c0 to be a uniform lower bound on S, which the text leaves implicit.

concepts.name: global methods in general relativity
concepts.definition: Arguments about the whole causal structure of a spacetime (Cauchy surfaces, spaces of causal curves, compactness, maximal curves) as opposed to local tensor calculations at a point.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the first margin note as the generalized form of the chapter's techniques, with Penrose, Wald and Hawking-Ellis as references.
prerequisites: compactness of the space of causal curves

concepts.name: Cauchy surface
concepts.definition: A spacelike hypersurface met exactly once by every inextendible timelike curve, so that data on it determine the whole spacetime; a spacetime possessing one is called globally hyperbolic.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as an assumption about the slice of fixed cosmic time, characterized loosely by its predictive power over the future, and used only to guarantee that maximal timelike curves exist.
concepts.notes: The text's description ('determines some future surface') is closer to the domain of dependence than to the precise definition.

concepts.name: domain of dependence
concepts.definition: The set of events p such that every inextendible causal curve through p crosses the surface S; conditions at such events are fixed entirely by data on S.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned alongside the Cauchy surface as the region in which the longest-curve guarantee holds.

concepts.name: compactness of the space of causal curves
concepts.definition: In a globally hyperbolic region, the set of timelike and null curves joining an event to a Cauchy surface is compact in a suitable topology, so proper length, being upper semicontinuous, attains a maximum.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in a margin note as the technicality underlying the existence of longest curves, glossed as 'no curves escape to infinity' with a pointer to Appendix C.
concepts.notes: The note says length is continuous; strictly it is upper semicontinuous, which still suffices.

concepts.name: existence of a maximal timelike curve
concepts.definition: For any event p in the domain of dependence of a Cauchy surface S there is a causal curve from S to p of greatest proper time; it is a timelike geodesic meeting S orthogonally with no focal point between S and p.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted at the chapter start as a consequence of the Cauchy property, then reused as one horn of the final contradiction.
prerequisites: compactness of the space of causal curves
maximal proper time of timelike geodesics

concepts.name: orthogonality of the shortest path to a surface
concepts.definition: A curve of minimal length from a point to a surface must be a geodesic that meets the surface at a right angle; otherwise sliding its foot along the surface shortens it.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in Euclidean 3-space with Fig. 50.1, where a slanted straight line is shown to be beaten by a perpendicular one.

concepts.name: normal geodesics
concepts.definition: Geodesics that leave a hypersurface along its unit normal; for a spacelike hypersurface in spacetime they are timelike geodesics starting at right angles to the slice.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in §50.1 for Euclidean surfaces and carried into spacetime in §50.2, where they become the world lines whose convergence is studied.
prerequisites: orthogonality of the shortest path to a surface

concepts.name: corner-cutting argument
concepts.definition: If a candidate extremal path to a surface has a kink, or can be replaced by a kinked path of equal length, smoothing the kink strictly improves it (shorter in Euclidean space, longer in proper time for timelike curves), so the candidate was not extremal.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated with Fig. 50.2: two normal geodesics cross at r, and a path that follows one to near r, shortcuts across, and follows the other to S beats the first.
concepts.notes: For timelike curves the reverse triangle inequality means smoothing a kink lengthens proper time; the book leaves this Lorentzian version implicit.

concepts.name: conjugate point
concepts.definition: A point along a geodesic where an infinitesimally neighbouring geodesic from the same starting point (or normal to the same surface, for a focal point) meets it again; past it the geodesic is no longer a local extremum of length.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from the Chapter 8 discussion of when a stationary action is a true minimum, and identified with the crossing point r of two normal geodesics.
concepts.notes: For curves starting on a surface the standard name is focal point; the book uses conjugate point for both.

concepts.name: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
concepts.definition: Among nearby timelike curves joining two events, the geodesic accumulates the most proper time, because acceleration reduces elapsed proper time in Lorentzian signature.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled at the start of §50.2 to justify replacing shortest with longest in every Euclidean statement.

concepts.name: proper-time function from a hypersurface
concepts.definition: A scalar field phi whose value at an event is the proper time elapsed along the normal geodesic from S to that event; its level sets are the hypersurfaces a fixed proper time away from S.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to measure how far along the normal geodesics each event lies, drawn as a stack of labelled sheets phi = 0, 1, 2, 3 (Fig. 50.3).
concepts.notes: That grad phi has unit norm is the Gauss lemma, assumed rather than proved.

concepts.name: hypersurface-orthogonal geodesic congruence
concepts.definition: A family of timelike geodesics filling a region, one through each event, whose unit tangent field is (up to sign) the gradient of a scalar, so the flow is everywhere orthogonal to a family of hypersurfaces and has zero rotation.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by setting the velocity 1-form equal to grad phi, raising the index with the metric, and showing the resulting field parallel-transports itself.
prerequisites: symmetry of the second covariant derivative of a scalar

concepts.name: symmetry of the second covariant derivative of a scalar
concepts.definition: For a torsion-free connection the second covariant derivatives of a scalar commute, so the covariant derivative of a gradient 1-form is a symmetric tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown in a margin note by writing the covariant derivative of the gradient and noting the connection coefficients are symmetric in their lower indices.

concepts.name: convergence of a geodesic congruence
concepts.definition: The scalar c = -u^mu_{;mu}, minus the divergence of the tangent field; it equals minus the fractional rate of change, per unit proper time, of the volume of a small comoving blob of the congruence, so c > 0 means world lines are drawing together.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined right after showing the normal field is geodesic, as the quantity whose evolution along the flow decides whether the congruence focuses.
concepts.notes: Conventional literature uses theta = u^mu_{;mu} = -c, as the exercises do.

concepts.name: Ricci identity
aliases: commutator of covariant derivatives on a vector
concepts.definition: The failure of second covariant derivatives of a vector field to commute is measured by the Riemann tensor contracted with that vector, so swapping derivative order costs a curvature term.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from eqn 35.13 and contracted on the first index with the differentiation index to bring in the Ricci tensor.

concepts.name: Ricci tensor
concepts.definition: The contraction R_{beta nu} = R^alpha_{beta alpha nu} of the Riemann tensor; contracted twice with a 4-velocity it measures the rate at which curvature shrinks a small ball of freely falling particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears from contracting the Ricci identity; interpreted in the text as the piece of curvature that makes volumes contract.

concepts.name: projection tensor orthogonal to the 4-velocity
concepts.definition: The symmetric tensor P_{alpha beta} = g_{alpha beta} + u_alpha u_beta, which removes the component of a vector along the unit timelike u and acts as the metric on the 3-space orthogonal to u; its trace is 3.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 39 to separate the velocity gradient into trace and trace-free parts; its properties are listed in a footnote and assigned as Exercise 50.1.

concepts.name: trace and trace-free decomposition of the velocity gradient
concepts.definition: Writing the symmetric, spatial tensor u_{alpha;nu} as its isotropic part -(c/3)P_{alpha nu} plus a remainder with zero trace; the two parts are orthogonal under full contraction.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 50.2 uses it to turn the awkward contracted square in the convergence equation into c^2/3 plus a non-negative piece.

concepts.name: trace inequality for the velocity gradient
concepts.definition: For the symmetric spatial velocity gradient of a hypersurface-orthogonal geodesic congruence, the full contraction u^{nu;alpha}u_{alpha;nu} is at least c^2/3, with equality exactly when the shear vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Result of Example 50.2: after the split, the trace-free square is dropped because it cannot be negative.
prerequisites: trace and trace-free decomposition of the velocity gradient
concepts.notes: In an eigenbasis this is the statement that the sum of squares of three numbers is at least one third of the square of their sum.

concepts.name: trace-reversed Einstein equation
concepts.definition: The field equation rewritten so the Ricci tensor is given directly by matter: R_{mu nu} = 8 pi (T_{mu nu} - (1/2) g_{mu nu} T) in units G = c = 1 without a cosmological constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Used, with velocity components contracted in, to turn the geometric Ricci term into a statement about matter.

concepts.name: weak energy condition
concepts.definition: The requirement that every observer measure a non-negative energy density, T_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu >= 0 for all timelike u.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited from Chapter 13 (where it appears only in a margin note, as a looser version of the dominant condition) as the reason the contracted Ricci term is non-negative, although that term really contains the trace-reversed stress tensor.
concepts.notes: Book error: the weak condition does not imply R_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu >= 0; the strong energy condition (Exercise 50.3) is what is needed.

concepts.name: strong energy condition
concepts.definition: The requirement (T_{mu nu} - (1/2) T g_{mu nu}) u^mu u^nu >= 0 for every timelike u, equivalently R_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu >= 0; for a perfect fluid it means rho + 3p >= 0 and rho + p >= 0. It encodes gravity being attractive for timelike geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by name only in Exercise 50.3 as the condition that guarantees focusing; implicitly it is what the §50.2 argument requires.
concepts.notes: Violated by a positive cosmological constant (rho + 3p = -2 rho_Lambda) and by an inflaton during slow roll.

concepts.name: focusing inequality
concepts.definition: Along a hypersurface-orthogonal timelike geodesic congruence satisfying the strong energy condition, the convergence grows at least as fast as c^2/3 per unit proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by combining the result of Example 50.1 with the trace inequality and the energy condition; read physically as gravity pulling world lines together.
prerequisites: trace inequality for the velocity gradient

concepts.name: focusing time bound
concepts.definition: If the initial convergence at S is c0 > 0, the focusing inequality forces c to become infinite no later than proper time tau = 3/c0 along each normal geodesic.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by integrating the differential inequality with c(0) = c0, in the same way as the elementary blow-up of dy/dx = y^2.

concepts.name: caustic
concepts.definition: The locus where neighbouring members of a congruence of curves meet, so that the convergence of the congruence diverges; familiar from optics as the bright envelope of focused light rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Named to interpret the divergence of c: world lines are forced to cross, which is harmless in itself but spoils maximality.

concepts.name: proof by contradiction via maximal curves
concepts.definition: The logical core of the theorem: a Cauchy surface guarantees a maximal curve to every event, yet a maximal curve must be a normal geodesic without crossings, and focusing forces crossings by 3/c0; hence no event can lie farther than 3/c0 from S.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled in the closing paragraphs of §50.2, with the key conclusion highlighted in a shaded box and then restated in plainer language.
prerequisites: existence of a maximal timelike curve

concepts.name: Friedmann-Robertson-Walker model
aliases: Robertson-Walker space filled with perfect fluid
concepts.definition: Homogeneous, isotropic cosmological spacetime with metric determined by a scale factor a(t) and curvature index, sourced by a perfect fluid according to the Friedmann equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in §50.3 as a good description of our Universe, to which the abstract theorem is applied.

concepts.name: comoving volume element
concepts.definition: The proper volume of a small region carried along with the cosmic fluid; in a Robertson-Walker universe it scales as the cube of the scale factor.
concepts.how_introduced: Used dimensionally to identify the convergence of the fluid world lines with minus the fractional rate of change of volume.

concepts.name: convergence of comoving Friedmann world lines
concepts.definition: For comoving dust in a Friedmann model the convergence is c = -3 a-dot/a = -3H, negative when the universe expands; the corresponding past-directed convergence is +3H.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from V proportional to a^3 and the reading of c as minus the fractional volume change rate.

concepts.name: Hubble parameter
concepts.definition: The fractional expansion rate H = a-dot/a of the scale factor; its present value H0 sets the Hubble time 1/H0.
concepts.how_introduced: Not named in the chapter, but the convergence formula c = -3 a-dot/a is three times it with a minus sign.

concepts.name: time reversal of the focusing argument
concepts.definition: Reversing the time orientation turns an expanding congruence (c < 0 to the future) into a converging one (c > 0 to the past), so the future-directed focusing theorem becomes a bound on how far back timelike curves extend.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the rescue after admitting the theorem cannot constrain an expanding universe's future.
prerequisites: convergence of comoving Friedmann world lines

concepts.name: smooth manifold assumption
concepts.definition: General relativity models spacetime as a smooth manifold on which fields are differentiable everywhere; places where that fails are not points of spacetime at all.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to explain where the curves traced back 3/c0 go: to a place that cannot be in the manifold, which must be cut out.

concepts.name: timelike geodesic incompleteness
concepts.definition: The existence of timelike geodesics that cannot be extended beyond a finite proper time within the spacetime manifold; the standard modern definition of a singular spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Conveyed pictorially as a timelike curve followed backwards that reaches a hole in the manifold and cannot continue (Fig. 50.4).
concepts.notes: The book says 'point'; for Friedmann models the boundary is a whole spacelike surface, reached by all comoving world lines at once.

concepts.name: Raychaudhuri equation
concepts.definition: The evolution equation for the velocity gradient of a timelike geodesic congruence; its trace says the expansion rate decreases because of its own square, the shear squared and the Ricci term along u, while only rotation can counteract the decrease.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Exercise 50.2 following Zee's derivation, presented as the conventional form of the §50.2 calculation.

concepts.name: velocity gradient tensor B
concepts.definition: The tensor B_{mu nu} = u_{mu;nu} of a geodesic congruence; acting on a connecting vector it gives the rate of change of that vector along the flow, and it is orthogonal to u in both slots.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Exercise 50.2 via connecting vectors W_i between neighbouring geodesics labelled by sigma^i.

concepts.name: expansion, shear and rotation decomposition
concepts.definition: Splitting B_{mu nu} into its trace theta (isotropic volume change), symmetric trace-free part sigma_{mu nu} (shape distortion at fixed volume) and antisymmetric part omega_{mu nu} (twisting of neighbouring world lines).
concepts.how_introduced: Given in Exercise 50.2 as the conventional split; the main text's gradient field has omega = 0 automatically.

concepts.name: zero rotation of a hypersurface-orthogonal congruence
concepts.definition: A geodesic congruence whose tangent is a gradient (orthogonal to a family of hypersurfaces) has vanishing rotation tensor, which removes the only term in the Raychaudhuri equation that opposes focusing.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in the symmetry of u_{nu;mu} used in §50.2; made explicit as the hypothesis of Exercise 50.3.

key_equations.name: Normal velocity field from the proper-time function
key_equations.meaning: The congruence of normal geodesics is described by the gradient of the proper-time-from-S function, normalized as a 4-velocity.
key_equations.symbols: phi proper time from S along the normal geodesic; u_mu components of the velocity 1-form

key_equations.name: Symmetry of the gradient's covariant derivative (margin note 3)
key_equations.meaning: Both terms are symmetric in mu and nu for a torsion-free connection, so u_{mu;nu} = u_{nu;mu}.

key_equations.name: Normal field is geodesic
key_equations.meaning: Symmetry lets the index order be swapped, turning the acceleration into the gradient of the constant norm, which vanishes; raising nu gives nabla_u u = 0.
key_equations.symbols: tilde u velocity 1-form; semicolon covariant derivative

key_equations.name: Convergence
key_equations.meaning: Minus the divergence of the congruence; positive when neighbouring world lines approach.
key_equations.symbols: c convergence (not the speed of light)

key_equations.meaning: Rate of change of convergence along the flow, written with the divergence differentiated again.

key_equations.name: Ricci identity (eqn 35.13)
key_equations.meaning: Commuting covariant derivatives of a vector produces curvature.
Contracting alpha with mu converts the commutator into the Ricci tensor.
Derivative order swapped at the cost of a Ricci term.
Product rule (integration by parts) moves the outer derivative off u^alpha; the first term contains the geodesic acceleration.
Geodesic property kills the total-derivative term, leaving a velocity-gradient square plus curvature. The text says the vanishing term is 'on the left' though it is on the right.

key_equations.name: Convergence evolution equation
key_equations.meaning: Convergence changes along the flow because of the self-contracted velocity gradient and the Ricci curvature; this is the trace of the Raychaudhuri equation for zero rotation, written in terms of c.

key_equations.name: Transverse projection tensor
key_equations.meaning: Metric on the 3-space orthogonal to u.

key_equations.name: Trace/trace-free split
key_equations.meaning: Isotropic part plus a remainder whose trace vanishes.

key_equations.name: Projection identities (margin note 5)
key_equations.meaning: Facts that make the cross terms in 50.11 vanish and fix the coefficient c^2/3. The note calls the first term's trace c; with the minus sign in 50.10 its trace is -c.
The square separates into the isotropic contribution c^2/3 and the square of the trace-free (shear) part.

key_equations.name: Trace inequality
key_equations.meaning: The shear square is non-negative because it lives in the positive-definite 3-space orthogonal to u.

key_equations.name: Contracted trace-reversed Einstein equation
key_equations.meaning: Converts the curvature term into matter; for a perfect fluid it equals 4 pi (rho + 3p).
key_equations.symbols: T trace of the energy-momentum tensor; G = c = 1

key_equations.name: Focusing inequality
key_equations.meaning: With a non-negative Ricci term, convergence grows at least quadratically: gravity focuses world lines.
Same inequality with the directional derivative written as a proper-time derivative along each geodesic.

key_equations.name: Blow-up bound
key_equations.meaning: Integrating from c(0) = c0 > 0 shows convergence must become infinite no later than tau = 3/c0.

key_equations.name: Maximal proper distance from S
key_equations.meaning: No event can be reached from S along a timelike curve of proper time longer than 3/c0. The shaded statement that no longest curve exists beyond 3/c0 is on printed p.550; the italic conclusion that spacetime cannot extend that far opens p.551.

key_equations.name: Convergence of an expanding Friedmann universe
key_equations.meaning: Comoving world lines diverge to the future; reversing time gives past convergence 3 a-dot/a.

key_equations.name: Past bound in Hubble units (not printed; follows from 50.16-50.17)
key_equations.meaning: The chapter's bound on the age of an SEC-obeying universe is the Hubble time, matching the tangent-line estimate of Chapter 18.

key_equations.name: Projection tensor (index-free)
key_equations.meaning: Slot-machine form of the projector orthogonal to a velocity u (Exercise 50.1); the printed ~u( , ) second factor has an extra slot.

key_equations.name: Projector orthogonal to a unit spacelike vector
key_equations.meaning: The sign flips because n.n = +1 rather than -1 (Exercise 50.1e).

key_equations.name: Evolution of connecting vectors
key_equations.meaning: Because connecting vectors are Lie dragged, their rate of change along the congruence is B acting on them.
key_equations.symbols: W_i connecting vectors; B velocity gradient

key_equations.name: Expansion scalar
key_equations.meaning: Trace of B, the fractional volume growth rate; theta = -c.

key_equations.name: Shear tensor
key_equations.meaning: Symmetric trace-free part: volume-preserving distortion.

key_equations.name: Rotation tensor
key_equations.meaning: Antisymmetric part: twisting of neighbouring world lines.
Full decomposition of the velocity gradient.

key_equations.name: Raychaudhuri equation (tensor form)
key_equations.meaning: How the whole velocity gradient changes along a geodesic congruence. Checked: consistent with the Riemann convention of eqn 50.4.
Trace of the square splits into shear, expansion and rotation pieces; rotation enters with the opposite sign.

key_equations.name: Raychaudhuri equation (scalar form)
key_equations.meaning: Expansion decreases because of expansion squared, shear and Ricci focusing; only rotation resists. Equivalent to 50.9 when omega = 0 and theta = -c.
With zero rotation the shear square, being spatial, can only help focusing.

key_equations.name: Strong energy condition
key_equations.latex: T_{\mu\nu}v^\mu v^\nu\ge\tfrac12 T\,v^\mu v_\mu\quad\text{for all timelike }\boldsymbol v
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent to R_{mu nu}v^mu v^nu >= 0; guarantees focusing of the congruence.

figures.label: Fig. 50.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A straight path that reaches the surface S obliquely is longer than one that arrives perpendicular to it.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing. A gently curved arc labelled S runs across the bottom. From a dot on the arc at lower left, a straight line labelled gamma climbs to a dot labelled p at upper right. A second, shorter curve labelled gamma-prime leaves gamma a little above the dot and comes down to S, with a small right-angle mark where it meets the arc. No axes or numbers.
figures.what_it_teaches: Point-to-surface minimizers must hit the surface orthogonally; any slanted approach can be improved.
concepts: orthogonality of the shortest path to a surface

redesign.idea: Point-to-surface distance explorer: a draggable point above an editable curved surface, with a slider for where the path lands.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags p and slides the foot point along S; a live readout shows the path length and the angle at the foot, and a small plot of length versus foot position marks its minimum exactly where the angle reads 90 degrees. A toggle switches to a 1+1 Minkowski panel where the same construction maximizes proper time from a curved spacelike slice.

figures.label: Fig. 50.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two perpendicular geodesics from S cross at r; from a point q beyond the crossing a shortcut across the corner and down the other geodesic beats the original path.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing. A curved surface S along the bottom carries two feet with right-angle marks. The left curve gamma rises from the left foot to a dot r and continues up to the right to a dot q. The right curve gamma-prime rises from the right foot, passes through r and continues up to the left. A short dashed segment links a tick on the r-to-q piece of gamma to a tick on gamma-prime just below r; a wavy arrow labelled t points at this dashed shortcut.
figures.what_it_teaches: After two normal geodesics cross, the one that continues is no longer extremal, because the corner at r can be cut; the crossing point plays the role of a conjugate (focal) point.

redesign.idea: Focal-point race: a concave surface emits a fan of normal geodesics that cross; a probe point q can be placed before or after a crossing, and competing paths to S are drawn with their lengths.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags q along one normal. Before the first crossing the normal path is the champion; once q passes a crossing, a highlighted corner-cut path appears and its length bar beats the normal path. A Lorentzian toggle redraws everything in a 1+1 spacetime diagram with proper-time bars, showing the corner-cut path now gains proper time.

figures.label: Fig. 50.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: The scalar phi records proper distance from S along the orthogonal geodesics; its level sets form a stack of parallel sheets.
figures.visual_description: Perspective sketch of four slightly wavy, parallel sheets stacked vertically and labelled phi = 0 (bottom), phi = 1, phi = 2 and phi = 3 (top). Short upward arrows sit on or between the sheets, and the arrow on the top sheet is labelled u^mu, indicating the normal velocity field crossing the level surfaces.
figures.what_it_teaches: The congruence can be encoded by a single scalar whose gradient is the unit normal velocity, which is what makes the velocity gradient symmetric and the flow geodesic.

redesign.idea: 3D normal congruence and its level sets: a bumpy spacelike sheet in a 2+1 spacetime launches unit normal world lines; surfaces of equal proper time are drawn as they evolve.
redesign.interaction: Learner sculpts the initial sheet's bumps (setting local c0) and turns up a matter-density knob. A proper-time slider advances the level sets; tubes of world lines visibly shrink, and where c blows up the level surfaces develop cusps (caustics) marked in red, with a readout comparing the time of blow-up to 3/c0.

figures.label: Fig. 50.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A singular point cannot belong to a smooth manifold, so it has to be removed.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn sketch of a slightly crumpled rectangular sheet with hatching and dots along its edges. A single curved line descends from the upper middle and ends at a small dashed circle in the lower half, representing a hole cut out of the sheet at which the curve stops.
figures.what_it_teaches: The singularity is not an event in spacetime; a timelike curve that runs into the excised region cannot be extended, which is what 'singular' means in the theorem.

redesign.idea: Tracing world lines back to the edge of spacetime: a Friedmann spacetime diagram in proper-time coordinates with comoving world lines converging toward the past, contrasted with a sheet-with-a-hole view.
redesign.interaction: Learner picks today's slice and H0, then drags a 'rewind' handle along any timelike curve; a proper-time counter runs and the curve halts at the boundary no later than 1/H0, with the bound line drawn. A second tab lets the learner try to continue the curve past the dashed hole in a sheet, which is refused, and a toggle shows that in Friedmann models the missing region is an entire spacelike edge rather than a single point. A dark-energy switch shows the bound can be evaded when rho + 3p < 0.

worked_examples.problem: Show that the unit field built from the gradient of the proper-time function is geodesic.
worked_examples.method: Use symmetry of the covariant derivative of a gradient to swap indices in the acceleration, recognize half the derivative of the constant norm u.u = -1, and raise the free index with a metric-compatible connection.
worked_examples.key_insight: Being a unit-norm gradient is enough to force geodesic motion; no equation of motion needs to be solved.
worked_examples.result: nabla_u u = 0, so u is tangent to all the normal geodesics.
concepts: symmetry of the second covariant derivative of a scalar

worked_examples.label: Example 50.1
worked_examples.problem: Find how the convergence c of the normal congruence changes along its own world lines.
worked_examples.method: Write the directional derivative of c as a double covariant derivative of u; use the Ricci identity (eqn 35.13) contracted on the derivative index to reorder the derivatives, producing a Ricci term; apply the product rule to pull out a term containing the geodesic acceleration, which vanishes.
worked_examples.key_insight: Reordering covariant derivatives is exactly where curvature enters, and the Ricci tensor (not the full Riemann tensor) controls volume change.
worked_examples.result: dc/dtau = u^nu_{;alpha} u^alpha_{;nu} + R_{beta nu}u^nu u^beta (eqns 50.8-50.9).

worked_examples.label: Example 50.2
worked_examples.problem: Bound from below the contracted square of the velocity gradient in terms of the convergence.
worked_examples.method: Split u_{alpha;nu} into -(c/3)P plus a trace-free remainder; multiply out, use P^{alpha beta}P_{alpha beta} = 3 and the orthogonality of P to the trace-free part so cross terms vanish; discard the non-negative square of the trace-free part.
worked_examples.key_insight: An isotropic part carries all of the trace, and any anisotropy (shear) only adds a positive amount, just as the mean square of three numbers exceeds the square of their mean.
concepts: trace and trace-free decomposition of the velocity gradient
trace inequality for the velocity gradient

worked_examples.problem: Solve the focusing inequality with the initial convergence c0 on S.
worked_examples.method: Rewrite dc/dtau >= c^2/3 as d(-1/c)/dtau >= 1/3, integrate from 0 to tau, and invert for positive c.
worked_examples.key_insight: A quadratic growth law blows up in finite time, so an initial positive convergence guarantees a caustic within a fixed proper time.

worked_examples.problem: Combine the geometric facts with the focusing bound to limit how far spacetime extends from S.
worked_examples.method: Assume an event p lies more than 3/c0 from S along a timelike curve; the Cauchy property supplies a maximal curve to p; maximal curves must be normal geodesics without crossings; focusing forces a crossing before 3/c0; contradiction.
worked_examples.key_insight: The singularity is inferred, not computed: two guaranteed properties are incompatible unless the spacetime ends.
worked_examples.result: No event is farther than 3/c0 from S along any timelike curve.
concepts: proof by contradiction via maximal curves
existence of a maximal timelike curve

worked_examples.problem: Evaluate the convergence for comoving matter in a Friedmann universe and decide whether the theorem applies.
worked_examples.method: Treat c as minus the fractional rate of change of a comoving volume, use V proportional to a^3, then reverse the time orientation.
worked_examples.key_insight: Expansion means divergence to the future but convergence to the past, so the theorem limits the past.
worked_examples.result: c = -3 a-dot/a; past-directed c0 = 3H0, so past timelike curves are shorter than 3/c0 = 1/H0 (the last equality is our step, not printed).
concepts: convergence of comoving Friedmann world lines
time reversal of the focusing argument

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Shortest path from a point to a wall in ordinary space
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: existence of a maximal timelike curve
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Everyday Euclidean facts (arrive perpendicular; do not continue past a crossing) are established first and then carried to spacetime by swapping shortest for longest.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The swap of inequality is justified only by appeal to the twin-paradox principle; in Lorentzian geometry there is no 'shortest' timelike curve at all, and kinks lengthen rather than shorten proper time.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen: Euclidean point-to-surface minimizer on the left, Minkowski point-to-slice maximizer on the right, driven by the same draggable handles.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Cutting the corner of an L-shaped route
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Once two normal geodesics cross, the traveller can shortcut near the crossing and ride the other geodesic home, showing the first is not optimal.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The book does not compare the lengths of the two geodesics below the crossing, which the full argument needs.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Let the learner draw their own shortcut near the crossing and watch the length counter drop.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Optical caustic of focused light rays
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The book names the blow-up of c a caustic, an envelope of the congruence that forces its members to cross. The optical picture of light rays piling up on an envelope is our gloss; the book does not mention optics.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Light rays focus by refraction or reflection; here world lines focus because matter curves spacetime, and the rays are timelike.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Show a coffee-cup caustic beside a congruence of world lines focusing under a matter-density slider.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravity as a converging lens for world lines
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The book reads the inequality as gravity being attractive and drawing world lines together along their length. The lens wording is our gloss on that reading.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only true if the strong energy condition holds; dark energy acts like a diverging lens.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Lens slider from converging (ordinary matter) to diverging (cosmological constant) acting on a bundle of world lines.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A sheet with a hole cut out
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A curve drawn on a sheet ends at a dashed excised region, conveying that the singular point is not part of spacetime and the curve cannot be continued.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Suggests a single point in space; the Friedmann singularity is reached by all comoving observers at the same cosmic time and is better pictured as a missing edge of the sheet.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph the hole into a torn-off bottom edge as the learner switches from a point-mass picture to a Friedmann picture.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Level sets of phi are drawn as parallel layers with the velocity arrow crossing them, like contour layers or wavefronts.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Layers stay smooth only until the congruence focuses; after that phi is not single-valued.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Huygens-style wavefront propagation from a curved sheet showing layers cusping at the caustic.

analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: time reversal of the focusing argument
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Expansion seen in reverse is contraction, so a theorem about converging world lines applies to the past of an expanding universe.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Reversing time changes no physics: the energy condition is time-symmetric. What must be redone is the bookkeeping, recomputing c with past-directed normals and applying the maximal-curve existence result to the past of the slice rather than its future.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Play/rewind button on a comoving-galaxy animation with a convergence gauge that flips sign.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Mean square versus square of the mean
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: trace inequality for the velocity gradient
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Our framing of Example 50.2: the three principal expansion rates have a sum fixed by c, and their squares are smallest when all three are equal.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Not stated this way in the book; requires the tensor to be symmetric and spatial.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Three sliders for principal rates with fixed sum; a bar for the sum of squares never dips below c^2/3.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Big Bang singularity is merely an artefact of assuming a perfectly homogeneous and isotropic universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The focusing argument uses only a Cauchy slice, an energy condition and positive past convergence everywhere; no exact symmetry is required, so small inhomogeneities cannot remove the past boundary.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Newtonian collapse, exact symmetry makes everything meet at one point, and slight asymmetry lets particles miss each other.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Geodesics in spacetime are the shortest paths, as in ordinary geometry.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Timelike geodesics maximize proper time; every Euclidean 'shortest' statement becomes 'longest' in spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Geodesics are introduced as straight lines, which are shortest in school geometry.
concepts: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: When the convergence of a congruence becomes infinite, spacetime itself is singular there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Infinite convergence only means neighbouring world lines cross, forming a caustic, which happens in perfectly smooth spacetime; the singularity follows from the contradiction with the existence of maximal curves, not from the caustic.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: A quantity blowing up usually signals a physical singularity.
concepts: proof by contradiction via maximal curves

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since galaxies are flying apart, the focusing theorem shows gravity is not attractive in cosmology or says nothing about our Universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The world lines diverge toward the future, so the theorem gives no future bound, but the same world lines converge toward the past, where the theorem applies.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The derivation assumed converging world lines, and our Universe expands.
concepts: time reversal of the focusing argument
convergence of comoving Friedmann world lines

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Positive energy density (the weak energy condition) is enough to guarantee focusing.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Focusing needs R_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu >= 0, the strong energy condition, which for a fluid is rho + 3p >= 0; a cosmological constant has positive energy density yet defocuses. The main text labels this the weak condition; Exercise 50.3 uses the correct one.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The contracted term looks like an energy density, and the text cites the weak condition.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The theorem proves that density and curvature become infinite at the Big Bang.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It proves only that past timelike curves end within finite proper time (incompleteness). Infinite density is a separate fact about Friedmann solutions; in principle curves could end for other reasons.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The word singularity evokes infinities, and the Friedmann solutions do have them.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Big Bang happened at a single point in space, like the excised dot in the figure.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In a Friedmann model every comoving world line reaches the singularity at the same cosmic time; it is a spacelike boundary of the whole universe, not a location within an existing space.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Fig. 50.4 shows a small hole, and 'explosion' imagery suggests a centre.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A longest timelike curve between a surface and an event always exists.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Existence relies on global hyperbolicity (a Cauchy surface) and compactness of the space of causal curves; in spacetimes with holes or without Cauchy surfaces maximal curves can fail to exist, which is exactly what the argument exploits.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Among a family of curves it seems obvious one must be longest.
concepts: existence of a maximal timelike curve
compactness of the space of causal curves

thought_experiments.name: Racing to a wall from beyond a crossing
thought_experiments.setup: Two perpendicular routes leave a curved wall and cross at r; a traveller at q farther along one route wants the quickest way back to the wall.
thought_experiments.lesson: Beyond a crossing the straight normal route is beaten by a corner-cut combination, so normal geodesics stop being optimal after they cross.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Game where the learner must find the best route to a curved wall from points placed before and after a focal point.

thought_experiments.name: Following a world line backwards into a hole
thought_experiments.setup: Starting on today's cosmic slice, trace any observer's history backwards in proper time.
thought_experiments.lesson: After at most 3/c0 the curve reaches a place that is not in the smooth manifold, so it cannot be continued: the Big-Bang singularity.
concepts: time reversal of the focusing argument
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rewind animation with a proper-time odometer that stops at the spacetime edge, next to the 1/H0 bound.

thought_experiments.name: Dust cloud with an initial squeeze
thought_experiments.setup: (Our construction, not in the book.) A ball of freely falling dust starts with its world lines converging at rate c0 on some slice, in a region obeying the strong energy condition.
thought_experiments.lesson: Gravity only amplifies the squeeze: the ball's world lines must meet within proper time 3/c0, whatever its shape (shear speeds this up).
thought_experiments.app_idea: 3D dust ball with adjustable initial convergence, shear and matter density; timer to collapse compared with 3/c0.

historical_notes.event: Epigraph from On the Nature of Things claiming the heavens and the world had a birth and are mortal.
historical_notes.significance: Frames the final chapter's topic, the beginning of the Universe, as a question with ancient philosophical roots.

historical_notes.event: Lecture notes on general relativity whose version of the singularity argument the chapter follows.
historical_notes.significance: Source of the streamlined orthogonal-geodesic proof sketch.

historical_notes.event: Monographs cited for the full global (causal-structure) techniques behind singularity theorems.
historical_notes.significance: Point readers to rigorous treatments of Cauchy surfaces, compactness and maximal curves.

historical_notes.event: The evolution equation for expansion of a geodesic congruence, named in Exercise 50.2 (the book gives no biography or date).
historical_notes.significance: The standard engine of singularity and focusing theorems.

applications_and_observations.details: Our Universe is modelled as close to a perfect-fluid Friedmann model; with the present slice as S and time reversed, every past timelike curve must end within finite proper time, so an initial singularity is expected.

applications_and_observations.topic: Hubble-time value of the bound (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: With past convergence c0 = 3H0 the bound is 1/H0. This is our computation, not printed in the chapter. A flat matter-only model has age 2/(3H0), comfortably inside the bound.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: H0 = 67.4 km/s/Mpc gives 1/H0 = 14.5 Gyr; H0 = 70 gives 14.0 Gyr; matter-only age 2/(3H0) = 9.7 Gyr; measured age about 13.8 Gyr (our estimates)

applications_and_observations.topic: Accelerating expansion and dark energy versus the energy condition (our note)
applications_and_observations.details: A positive cosmological constant has p = -rho, so rho + 3p = -2 rho < 0 and the strong energy condition fails; the chapter's hypothesis is therefore violated in the present dark-energy era and during inflation. The measured age still happens to satisfy t0 < 1/H0, and later theorems (e.g. Borde-Guth-Vilenkin) address past incompleteness without that energy condition. Not discussed in the book.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: t0 H0 about 0.95 for Planck-like parameters (our estimate)

notation_and_conventions.convention: (-,+,+,+): a unit timelike velocity has u^mu u_mu = -1.
Geometric units G = c = 1, so the field equation carries 8 pi.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The letter c is reused for convergence; do not confuse it with the speed of light.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Main text uses c = -u^mu_{;mu} (positive when focusing); the exercises use theta = u^mu_{;mu} = -c.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Most GR literature uses theta; translate signs when comparing 50.9 with 50.26.

notation_and_conventions.convention: u^alpha_{;nu mu} means differentiate with respect to nu first, then mu; with this order the commutator equals +R^alpha_{beta mu nu}u^beta (eqn 35.13).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Index order must be tracked when contracting to the Ricci tensor R_{beta nu} = R^alpha_{beta alpha nu}.

notation_and_conventions.convention: nabla_u, written D/dtau along a proper-time-parametrized curve.
Bold letters for vectors (u), bold with tilde for 1-forms (u-tilde); index-free slot notation g( , ) in Exercise 50.1.
P_{alpha beta} = g_{alpha beta} + u_alpha u_beta for timelike u; g - n n for unit spacelike n.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other texts call it h_{alpha beta}.

notation_and_conventions.convention: phi proper time from S, S the Cauchy slice, tau proper time along a normal geodesic, c0 convergence at S; in exercises B_{mu nu} = u_{mu;nu}, sigma shear, omega rotation, W_i connecting vectors (following Zee).

margin_notes.summary: Credits Geroch's 1972 lecture notes (published 2013) for the form of the argument and names the general approach as global techniques, citing Penrose, Wald and Hawking-Ellis.

Explains that longest curves exist because the set of causal curves from an event in the domain of dependence to S is compact (no curve escapes to infinity), so length attains a maximum; points to Appendix C.
Shows the covariant derivative of a gradient is symmetric by writing it with second partial derivatives and symmetric connection coefficients.
Refers back to Chapter 39 for the transverse projection operator.
Lists the five facts behind the trace split (symmetry of P and u_{alpha;beta}; trace of each part; P.P = 3; P contracted with u_{alpha;beta} = -c) and defers their proofs to the exercises.
Lucretius epigraph on the heavens having had a birth.

difficulty.notes: Only seven pages, but it compresses a research-level theorem. The local calculation (Examples 50.1-50.2) needs confident index gymnastics with the Ricci identity and projection tensors; the global ingredients (Cauchy surfaces, domains of dependence, compactness, focal points) are asserted rather than developed, and the logic runs by contradiction. Several small printed slips (weak versus strong energy condition, 'left' for 'right', a sign in note 5, a garbled summary bullet) can confuse careful readers.

teaching_gems.gem: Prove the key extremal facts in flat Euclidean space with pictures, then transport them to spacetime by replacing shortest with longest.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners already trust perpendicular-is-shortest; the only new idea is the reversed inequality, which they know from the twin paradox.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Dual-panel Euclidean/Minkowski construction where the same drag gestures minimize length on one side and maximize proper time on the other.

teaching_gems.gem: Encode the congruence as the gradient of a proper-time function so geodesic motion and symmetry of u_{mu;nu} follow in one line.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces the machinery of vorticity and Frobenius with a single visible fact: gradients have symmetric derivatives.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draw level sets of phi; arrows auto-orient perpendicular to them; a 'twist' slider that breaks the gradient property shows arrows no longer normal to any surfaces.

teaching_gems.gem: Split the velocity gradient into isotropic and trace-free parts to turn a messy contraction into c^2/3 plus a positive leftover.
teaching_gems.why_effective: It is the tensor version of 'mean square is at least the square of the mean', an inequality learners can check with three numbers.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Three principal-rate sliders with fixed sum; live bars for sum of squares and c^2/3, with the gap labelled shear.

teaching_gems.gem: Integrate a Riccati-type inequality to get guaranteed finite-time blow-up of convergence.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A one-line ODE produces a hard universal number (3/c0), turning qualitative 'gravity attracts' into a quantitative deadline.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plot c(tau) for chosen c0 and Ricci/shear contributions; all curves hit the vertical asymptote at or before 3/c0.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive the singularity by contradiction between existence of longest curves and their impossibility past the focusing time.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows students that singularities can be deduced from global logic rather than by computing a blow-up in a specific solution.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Logic-flow card game: learner arranges premise cards (Cauchy, maximal curve, normal, no crossing, focusing) and sees which conclusion is forced.

teaching_gems.gem: Stage the cosmological application as failure then rescue by reversing time.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The apparent dead end makes learners check the sign of c themselves and remember why the theorem bounds the past, not the future.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Expanding-universe animation with a convergence dial; pressing rewind flips the dial positive and draws the 3/c0 bound backward from today.

teaching_gems.gem: Read convergence as minus the fractional change of comoving volume, giving c = -3H for Friedmann dust.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects an abstract divergence to a number cosmologists quote, and makes the bound 1/H0 immediately computable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Comoving cube whose volume readout and -d ln V/dt update as the learner changes H.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text says the weak energy condition makes R_{mu nu}u^mu u^nu non-negative, but that term is (T - (1/2)gT)uu, whose positivity is the strong energy condition (the one Exercise 50.3 correctly names).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners will believe positive energy density suffices and be puzzled that a cosmological constant (positive rho) accelerates expansion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the strong energy condition in §50.2, compute rho + 3p for dust, radiation and Lambda, and show which obey it.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Non-negativity of the trace-free square in Example 50.2 is asserted without saying why; it holds because that tensor is symmetric and orthogonal to u, so it lives in a positive-definite 3-space.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: In Lorentzian signature contractions can be negative, so the claim looks unjustified.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Go to the rest frame of u, show the tensor has only spatial components, and write the contraction as a sum of squares.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The unit norm of grad phi (Gauss lemma) is taken for granted, and u_mu = grad_mu phi with u.u = -1 actually makes phi decrease along u, a sign glossed over.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful readers find that dphi/dtau = u^mu u_mu = -1, apparently contradicting phi being elapsed proper time.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use u_mu = -grad_mu phi for future-directed u, and note the sign does not affect symmetry or the geodesic result.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The theorem needs c0 to be a positive lower bound on the convergence everywhere on S; the text treats c0 as a single number without saying so.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: It is unclear why a universe with some locally diverging regions would still be singular.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define c0 = inf over S of the convergence and note that for a near-Friedmann universe this is close to 3H0 everywhere.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The corner-cutting argument is given only in Euclidean space; the Lorentzian version (smoothing a kink in a timelike curve increases proper time) and the case analysis comparing the two geodesics below the crossing are skipped. Infinite convergence implying an actual crossing (focal point) is also asserted.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The key step 'crossing implies not maximal' may feel like hand-waving in spacetime.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the reverse triangle inequality on a Minkowski diagram, then cite the focal-point theorem from Wald or Hawking-Ellis.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: What is proved is past timelike incompleteness, but the text and Fig. 50.4 speak of a singular point cut from the manifold; for Friedmann models the boundary is spacelike and reached by all observers at once, and the theorem says nothing directly about infinite curvature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Reinforces the popular picture of the Big Bang as an explosion at a point.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair the hole picture with a spacetime diagram showing a missing bottom edge, and distinguish incompleteness from curvature blow-up.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The applicability to our actual Universe ignores dark energy and inflation, both of which violate the strong energy condition, and ignores quantum-gravity limits discussed in Chapter 49.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The closing claim that the singularity is inevitable sounds stronger than modern cosmology supports.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a caveat box: late-time acceleration and inflation evade the hypothesis; mention Borde-Guth-Vilenkin-style incompleteness results and that classical GR is not trusted at Planck densities.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The chapter never evaluates 3/c0 for our Universe, missing the neat result that it equals the Hubble time 1/H0 already met in Chapter 18.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The bound stays abstract; learners cannot sanity-check it against the known age.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Plug in c0 = 3H0 and compare 1/H0 of about 14.5 Gyr with the 13.8 Gyr age.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed slips: 'first term on the left' after 50.7 should be on the right; note 5(ii) gives the first term's trace as c though with the minus sign it is -c; 'scales varies' in §50.3; the second summary bullet omits 'longest' and so reads as self-contradictory; the reading copy renders a-dot in §50.3 as a fraktur c.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Small sign and wording errors derail learners checking each step.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Correct these in any rewrite and state the summary as: no event lies farther than 3/c0 from S along any timelike curve.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Cauchy surface and domain of dependence are defined in a single informal sentence, and the compactness note claims length is continuous (it is upper semicontinuous).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners lack the causal-structure background to see why maximal curves exist, which is half of the proof.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Give a Minkowski example of a Cauchy slice and a counterexample (spacetime with a point removed) where maximal curves fail to exist.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'Friedmann models all start at a = 0, but they are perfectly smooth and symmetric. If the real Universe is lumpy, could matter have missed itself and bounced?' Let the learner guess before revealing that a symmetry-free argument exists.
Before any tensors, check two warm-up facts: what is the shortest path from a point to a curved wall, and which of two twins ages more. The whole proof rests on combining these.

Recommended order: (1) Euclidean normals and corner cutting; (2) longest instead of shortest; (3) proper-time function and its gradient; (4) define c and interpret its sign as volume shrinking; (5) the ODE dc/dtau >= c^2/3 and its blow-up, taken as given first; (6) the contradiction; (7) the cosmological application and time reversal; (8) only then return to Examples 50.1-50.2 for the derivation.

Check for understanding: ask why a caustic by itself is not a singularity. Good answer: crossing world lines are allowed; the problem is that crossing destroys maximality, which the Cauchy surface demands.
Check: ask the learner to compute c for an expanding Friedmann universe and say whether the theorem bounds the future or the past, and why.
Numerical anchor: have the learner plug c0 = 3H0 and H0 of about 70 km/s/Mpc into 3/c0 to get about 14 Gyr, then compare with the 13.8 Gyr age.
Correct the energy-condition slip proactively: the needed condition is rho + 3p >= 0 (strong), not rho >= 0 (weak). Ask what happens for a cosmological constant.

For the trace inequality, use three numbers: if three principal expansion rates must add to -c, the sum of their squares is smallest when they are equal, giving c^2/3. Then show shear only adds to it.

Common learner question: 'Does this prove the density was infinite?' Answer: it proves world lines cannot be extended to the past beyond a finite proper time; the infinities come from the explicit models and may be modified by quantum gravity.

Common learner question: 'Where did the Big Bang happen?' Use Fig. 50.4 with care: the singularity is not a place inside space; in Friedmann models every comoving observer's past ends at the same cosmic time.
Common learner question: 'Why does rotation matter?' Point to Exercise 50.2: rotation is the only Raychaudhuri term that resists focusing, and gradient flows have none.
Advanced learners: connect to the Raychaudhuri equation in theta notation, to Penrose's null version for black holes, and to why inflation and dark energy evade the hypotheses.
